message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Common isotope** | ^1H (protium) – 99.98 % natural abundance |
| **Other stable isotopes** | ^2H (deuterium, 0.02 %) and ^3H (tritium, radioactive, ~10⁻⁵ %) |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average weighted by natural isotopic composition) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Valence electrons** | 1 |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 27.211 eV (2625 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because H tends to lose its single electron rather than gain one) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) at 1 atm |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) at 1 atm |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 kg m⁻³) |
| **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas |
| **Bond type** | Covalent (single bond in H₂) |
| **Molecular formula** | H₂ (most common form) |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar molecule) |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, acids, and many nonmetals; reacts explosively with oxygen or air under right conditions |
| **Uses** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), rocket propellant, ammonia synthesis (Haber process), refining petroleum, producing methanol, as a reducing agent in metallurgy, in semiconductor manufacturing, in medical imaging (MRI contrast agents). |
| **Safety notes** | Extremely flammable; low ignition energy (~0.02 J); forms explosive mixtures with air (4–75 % H₂ in air). Requires careful handling and proper ventilation. |

---

### Key Takeaways

* Hydrogen is the lightest element, existing naturally mainly as diatomic gas (H₂).
* It has only one proton and one electron in its most common isotope, giving it unique quantum mechanical behavior.
* Its physical constants (boiling/melting points, density) make it extremely cold and light compared to other gases.
* Chemically, it is highly versatile—forming covalent bonds with almost all elements, participating in acid–base chemistry, and serving as a key component in industrial processes such as ammonia production and petroleum refining.
* Safety is paramount due to its high flammability and potential for forming explosive mixtures with air.
